questions.scenario: Each item in a container includes a property named embedding that contains 1,536 floating-point numbers. The container uses the default indexing policy. Queries never filter on the embedding property by using equality or range filters.
questions.question: You need to reduce the RU charge of write operations. What should you do?

options.text: Add /embedding/* to excludedPaths in the indexing policy
options.why: Correct. Excluding the path stops the range index from indexing every element of the array, which lowers write RUs.

options.text: Add /embedding/? to includedPaths in the indexing policy
options.why: This keeps the property in the range index, which does not reduce write cost.

options.text: Change the default consistency level to Strong
options.why: Strong consistency increases read cost and latency and does not reduce indexing cost on writes.

options.text: Add a composite index on /embedding and /id
options.why: A composite index adds more indexing work instead of reducing it.

questions.explanation: By default every path is indexed. Excluding large paths that are not used in filters reduces the RU charge of writes.

questions.question: A query includes ORDER BY c.category ASC, c.price ASC and returns an error that states that the order by query does not have a corresponding composite index. What should you add to the indexing policy?

options.text: A spatial index on /price
options.why: Spatial indexes support geospatial queries, not sorting.

options.text: A vector index on /category
options.why: A vector index supports similarity search, not ORDER BY on scalar properties.

options.text: A composite index on /category ascending and /price ascending
options.why: Correct. ORDER BY on multiple properties requires a composite index with matching paths and order.

options.text: An excluded path for /category/?
options.why: Excluding the path makes the query more expensive and does not provide the required composite index.

questions.explanation: Queries that sort by more than one property need a composite index whose paths and sort order match the query.

questions.question: A chat application stores conversation history in Azure Cosmos DB. After a user sends a message, that user must always see the message when the history is read again. Other users do not need to see the message immediately. You must minimize read cost. Which consistency level should you use?

options.text: Strong
options.why: Strong meets the requirement but reads cost about twice as many RUs and add latency.

options.text: Bounded staleness
options.why: Bounded staleness reads also cost about twice as many RUs, which does not minimize cost.

options.text: Eventual
options.why: Eventual does not guarantee that users read their own writes.

options.text: Session
options.why: Correct. Session guarantees read-your-own-writes within a session and uses single-replica reads.

questions.explanation: Session consistency, the default, guarantees that a client reads its own writes at the same RU cost as the weaker levels.

questions.question: An Azure Cosmos DB account uses Session as the default consistency level. Which TWO statements are true?

options.text: A client can override the consistency level to Eventual for its reads
options.why: Correct. A client or request can relax the consistency level to a weaker one than the account default.

options.text: A client can override the consistency level to Strong for its reads
options.why: Clients can only weaken the default. Changing to Strong requires changing the account default.

options.text: Reads at Strong or Bounded staleness consistency cost about twice the RUs of reads at Session consistency
options.why: Correct. Strong and Bounded staleness read from two replicas, which doubles the read RU cost.

options.text: Session consistency guarantees that all clients in all regions see every write immediately
options.why: That describes Strong consistency. Session guarantees read-your-own-writes within a session only.

questions.explanation: The account default can be relaxed per client or request. Strong and Bounded staleness reads cost about twice as much because they use two replicas.

questions.question: An application frequently receives HTTP status code 429 from Azure Cosmos DB during peak hours. What does this status code indicate?

options.text: The partition key value in the request is not valid
options.why: An invalid request returns a 400-series error such as 400 Bad Request, not 429.

options.text: The requests need more Request Units per second than the provisioned throughput allows
options.why: Correct. 429 Too Many Requests means the request rate exceeded the available RU/s. The SDK retries after the suggested wait time.

options.text: The item that was requested does not exist
options.why: A missing item returns 404 Not Found.

options.text: The identity does not have a data plane role assignment
options.why: Missing permissions return 403 Forbidden.

questions.explanation: 429 indicates rate limiting. Increase throughput, use autoscale, or reduce the RU cost of operations.
